newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Palestinians reject Israeli change on Hebron.
newsitem.headline: Palestinians reject Israeli change on Hebron.

text.p: Palestinians on Friday firmly rejected Israel's first public demand to change part of the previously-agreed deal on withdrawing from most of the West Bank city of Hebron.

"Our position is firm. We are not ready to renegotiate any part of the agreement," negotiator Hassan Asfour said after Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai said Palestinian police in Hebron should not be allowed to carry the rifles specified in the agreement signed by the previous Israeli government.

Mordechai confirmed in an interview with the Jerusalem Post Israel wanted changes, although Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had denied Palestinian charges he wants to renegotiate the Hebron agreement.
He was asked if Israel was demanding at the U.S.-mediated negotations that Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) police due to be stationed in Hebron carry only pistols.
"Yes," he replied, "We understandably want to reduce the scale and types of weapons to reduce the dangers that could likely happen."

Israel's previous government, ousted by the right-wing Netanyahu in May elections, signed an agreement in September 1995 that said up to 400 Palestinian policemen armed with 200 pistols and 100 rifles would deploy in parts of Hebron which will be handed over to the PLO by Israel.

The Hebron talks that began last Sunday -- decided at an emergency summit in Washington after Israeli-Palestinian violence in September killed 60 Palestinians and 15 Israelis -- are supposed to deal with ways to implement the existing agreement.
"This shows that the Israelis want to renegotiate the essence of the agreement, which we are not willing to do," Asfour said of Mordechai's comments.
"Mr Mordechai should study the issue not from the point of view of ideological intransigence but from the practical needs of having a strong Palestinian police in Hebron," Asfour said.
Despite the differences in the talks -- which Palestinian President Yasser Arafat said on Thursday had shown no progress -- Palestinians gave mixed assessments on the prospects for a breakthrough.

Asfour said there had been no progress in the negotiations but Palestinian West Bank security chief Jibril Rajoub said he was "100 percent" certain Israel and the PLO would soon agree on the long-delayed Israeli redeployment in Hebron.

Under the original agreement, Israel was to have withdrawn nearly seven months ago from most of the West Bank city where 400 Jewish settlers live in heavily-armed compounds amidst 100,000 Arabs. Israeli soldiers are to remain in some areas to guard the hardline settlers.

The redeployment was delayed after Moslem suicide bombers killed 59 people in Israel early this year and then was frozen when the new Israel government took office in June and said it needed better security for the settlers.

U.S. Special Mideast Coordinator Dennis Ross, mediating the talks, said on Thursday Israel and the PLO had agreed to move negotiations to the Red Sea resorts of Eilat, in Israel, and nearby Taba, in Egypt.

Ross said the change in venue would increase the pace of negotiations. Palestinans sources said formal talks, recessed from Thursday, would resume on Monday in Taba. However, lower-level contacts continued on Friday.
